title: Paraspinal Loading Dose Followed by Biweekly Subcutaneous NVG-291 with Adjuvant Thymosin β4 in Chronic Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury: 1st study of A Prospective, Open-Label, Single Arm Case Series of Ten Patients
content: Background. Chronic traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) produces persistent neurological impairment for which no regenerative pharmacotherapy is approved. NVG-291, a systemically deliverable peptide mimetic that modulates the chondroitin sulphate proteoglycan receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase σ (PTPσ), has shown functional benefit in preclinical SCI models and in a randomised Phase 1b/2a study using daily subcutaneous dosing. Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) is an actin-sequestering peptide with anti-inflammatory, angiogenic and pro-remyelinating properties in central nervous system injury models. Neither agent is licensed for SCI, and the two have not previously been reported in combination in humans. Objective. To describe the safety profile and the observed change in motor and ambulatory function associated with a single paraspinal loading dose of NVG-291 followed by 12 months of biweekly subcutaneous NVG-291 and Tβ4 in a consecutive series of patients with chronic traumatic SCI, and to define the hypotheses that a future controlled trial would need to test. Design, setting and participants. Prospective, open-label, single-arm, single-centre case series without a control group, conducted at NuRaX Clinic, Baku, Azerbaijan, in collaboration with Ege Hospital, Baku, between April 2024 and May 2025. Ten consecutive adults with chronic traumatic SCI at neurological levels C4–L4 were treated: three cervical, five thoracic and two lumbar. All were graded American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS) A or B at baseline. Intervention. A single paraspinal administration of NVG-291 3.5 mg on day 0, followed by subcutaneous NVG-291 0.9 mg and Tβ4 0.25 mg every 14 days for 12 months (26 maintenance doses of each agent), corresponding to a cumulative exposure of approximately 26.9 mg of NVG-291 (including the loading dose) and 6.5 mg of Tβ4 per patient. All patients received concurrent individualised rehabilitation throughout. Outcome measures. Because the series was uncontrolled and exploratory, no confirmatory primary endpoint was defined. Pre-specified descriptive outcomes were Medical Research Council (MRC) motor grade in the index muscle group, presence of voluntary knee locking, 10-metre walk test (10MWT) time with a walker, standing endurance, light-touch and pin-prick sensation, muscle bulk, functional independence, and treatment-emergent adverse events, assessed at baseline, 6 months and 12 months. Results. All ten patients completed 12 months of treatment; no patient withdrew or was lost to follow-up. MRC grade in the index muscle group increased by 2 points in six patients and by 1 point in two, and was unchanged in the two lumbar patients (median change 2 points, Wilcoxon signed-rank exact p = 0.008, n = 8 non-tied pairs; exploratory and uncorrected). In the three cervical patients, hand MRC grade rose from 2 to 4 (one patient) and from 1 to 3 (two patients). Three of five thoracic patients (T-2, T-4, T-5) improved from MRC 2 to 4, acquired voluntary bilateral knee locking and progressed from being unable to take an independent step at baseline to completing a 10-metre walk with a walker; their 10MWT times shortened from 110–132 s at 6 months to 55–72 s at 12 months. The two remaining thoracic patients improved from MRC 2 to 3 without acquiring knee locking. Both lumbar patients acquired voluntary knee locking within 3 months and improved 10MWT time from 75 and 59 s at 6 months to 55 and 48 s at 12 months. Across the five ambulatory patients, median 10MWT time fell from 110 s to 60 s (exact p = 0.063). Light-touch score improved in all five thoracic patients; pin-prick score improved in four and fell by 10 points in one (T-5) without change in AIS grade. Treatment-emergent adverse events were limited to mild, self-limiting injection-site erythema and localised skin reactions in one participant and mild fever after the paraspinal injection in one further participant (2 of 10 participants; all Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 1). No serious adverse event, neurological deterioration, treatment-related hospitalisation or death occurred. Conclusions. In this uncontrolled series of ten patients with chronic traumatic SCI, combined paraspinal and biweekly subcutaneous NVG-291 with adjuvant Tβ4, delivered alongside intensive rehabilitation, was associated with improvement in motor grade and walking performance and was well tolerated over 12 months. These observations cannot be attributed to the peptides: the absence of a control group, of blinded adjudication of all outcomes, and of any adjustment for concurrent rehabilitation makes rehabilitation effect, observer expectation and regression to the mean equally plausible explanations. The findings are hypothesis-generating only and require testing in a randomised, sham-controlled, multicentre trial with blinded International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI) assessment.
